mcq: The questions follow the order of the syllabus: environment basics first, laws and ethics at the end.
Many questions repeat word for word — go through the 'Asked again and again' list on the course page first.
Answer every question: leave nothing blank on the OMR sheet.
For 'which is NOT' questions, cross out the three that fit — the one left is the answer.
Make a one-page list of years (Acts, conventions), places (NGT benches, wetlands, biogeographic zones) and names (movements) and revise it on exam day.

topics.name: Global Issues: Climate, Ozone, Acid Rain & Disasters
topics.summary: Greenhouse gases, climate change, ozone depletion, acid rain, international conventions and natural disasters.
points: Greenhouse gases: carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, CFCs and water vapour. Sulphur dioxide is not a greenhouse gas.
Ozone layer is in the stratosphere; CFCs deplete it. Ultraviolet radiation causes skin cancer and cataract.
Normal rain is slightly acidic (pH about 5.6); acid rain has pH below 5.6 — caused by SO₂ and NOₓ.
Vienna Convention (1985) and Montreal Protocol (1987): ozone layer. UNFCCC (1992, Rio): climate. Kyoto Protocol (1997), Paris Agreement (2015).
IPCC (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change) was set up in 1988.
Basel Convention: transboundary movement of hazardous wastes. Ramsar (1971): wetlands. CITES: trade in endangered species.

Disasters: earthquakes, floods, cyclones, droughts, landslides, tsunamis. Asia is the region most prone to natural calamities. Seismic Zone V (highest risk) includes the North-East, Kachchh and parts of the Himalaya.
mistakes: Confusing the Montreal Protocol (ozone) with the Kyoto Protocol (greenhouse gases).

topics.name: Biodiversity & Its Conservation
topics.summary: Levels and values of biodiversity, India as a megadiverse country, biogeographic zones, threats, invasive species, in-situ and ex-situ conservation.
points: Levels: genetic, species and ecosystem diversity.
Values: direct use (consumptive, productive), indirect use (ecosystem services such as pollination, watershed protection), non-use (option, bequest, existence).

India is one of the 17 megadiverse countries, with about 2.4% of the world's land and 7–8% of recorded species; it has 4 of the world's biodiversity hotspots (Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats–Sri Lanka, Sundaland/Nicobar).
India has 10 biogeographic zones; the Deccan Peninsula is the largest; the Trans-Himalaya zone is in Ladakh.
Tropical rain forests hold more than half of the world's plant species.

Threats: habitat loss, invasive species, pollution, over-exploitation, climate change. Invasive species in India: Parthenium (congress weed — causes skin allergy), water hyacinth, Lantana, Prosopis (mesquite).
In-situ conservation: national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biosphere reserves (core, buffer, transition zones). UNESCO's MAB = Man and the Biosphere programme.
Ex-situ conservation: zoos, botanical gardens, seed and gene banks (genetic insurance), tissue culture, artificial insemination.

topics.name: Pollution & Waste Management
topics.summary: Air, water, noise and soil pollution, pollution standards and tests, solid and hazardous waste management.
points: Primary pollutants are emitted directly (SO₂, CO, NOₓ, hydrocarbons, particulates); secondary pollutants form in the air (ozone, PAN, smog, sulphuric and nitric acid).
Natural pollutants: pollen, volcanic gases, dust, decaying organic matter.
Point sources (chimneys, discharge pipes) vs non-point sources (run-off from farms and cities).
RSPM/PM10 standard in India: 60 µg/m³ (annual average).
Taj Trapezium Zone around Agra protects the Taj Mahal from air pollution (Mathura refinery, foundries, brick kilns, glass factories).
Water quality: BOD and COD (organic pollution), TDS = total dissolved solids, MPN test detects coliform bacteria such as E. coli.
Eutrophication: nutrient overload causes algal blooms. Biomagnification: toxins (DDT, mercury) increase up the food chain.
Noise is measured in decibels, dB(A).
Sludge gas (biogas) is mostly methane.

Waste hierarchy: reduce, reuse, recycle, recover, dispose. Landfill is disposal, not a waste-minimisation method. Treatment: physical (sedimentation, filtration), chemical, biological (composting, activated sludge).
Disasters: Minamata (mercury), Itai-itai (cadmium), Bhopal gas tragedy 1984 (methyl isocyanate).

topics.name: Natural Resources: Water, Land & Energy
topics.summary: Water on earth and its cycle, soils and erosion, forests, minerals, conventional and non-conventional energy.
points: About 97.5% of the earth's water is salt water and 2.5% fresh; most fresh water is frozen — less than 1% is readily accessible.
Sublimation: ice changes directly to vapour. Transpiration: water loss as vapour from plants.
Aquifer: a water-bearing layer of rock or soil that stores groundwater.
Black (regur) soil is found in the Deccan and Malwa plateau. Ravines form by gully erosion from running water.
Resources: renewable (forests, wildlife, water) vs non-renewable (minerals, fossil fuels).
Conventional energy: coal, petroleum, natural gas, (large) hydro, atomic. Non-conventional: solar, wind, geothermal, tidal, biomass.
China is the world's largest coal producer. Bombay High is India's largest oil-producing field.
A biomass gasifier converts solid fuel into gaseous fuel. Hydrogen is the best fuel for a fuel cell.
Joint Forest Management began in West Bengal (Arabari).

topics.name: Ecosystem Structure, Energy Flow & Cycles
topics.summary: Producers, consumers and decomposers, trophic levels and food chains, energy flow, biogeochemical cycles, succession.
points: Producers (autotrophs) make food; consumers are herbivores (primary), carnivores (secondary, tertiary); decomposers are saprophytes (saprotrophs).
Chemosynthetic bacteria are autotrophs.
Food chains: grazing and detritus. Only about 10% of energy passes to the next trophic level (Lindeman's 10% law); the pyramid of energy is always upright.
Biogeochemical cycles: gaseous (nitrogen, carbon, oxygen) and sedimentary (phosphorus, sulphur). The atmosphere is the main nitrogen reservoir; sediments hold most sulphur.
Ecological succession: pioneer community → intermediate (seral) stages → climax community.
Niche: an organism's role; habitat: where it lives; ecotone: transition zone between two ecosystems.
Estuaries are transition zones of very high productivity.

topics.name: Forest, Grassland, Desert & Aquatic Ecosystems
topics.summary: Types of forests and their features, desert adaptations, lentic and lotic waters, aquatic organisms, wetlands and seas.
points: Coniferous (boreal) forests: spruce, fir, pine; soil is acidic and poor in minerals.
Temperate deciduous forests shed leaves in winter; tropical rain forests have the highest diversity.
Desert animals conserve water — some excrete very concentrated urine.
Lentic (standing) waters: lakes, ponds, wetlands, reservoirs. Lotic (flowing) waters: rivers and streams.
Aquatic life: plankton (drifting), nekton (swimming), neuston (air–water surface), benthos (bottom), periphyton (attached to surfaces).
Average salinity of sea water is about 35 parts per thousand (3.5%).
Wetlands: Chilika (Odisha), Harike (Punjab), Sambhar (Rajasthan), Loktak (Manipur), Sundarbans (West Bengal).

topics.name: Environment, Population & Sustainable Development
topics.summary: Components of the environment, human–environment ideas (determinism, possibilism), population growth, carrying capacity, SDGs.
points: Environment: all biotic (living) and abiotic (non-living) surroundings.
Components: lithosphere (land), hydrosphere (water), atmosphere (air), biosphere (life), cryosphere (ice).
Natural environment (forests, lakes) vs human-modified (crop fields, plantations) vs human-made (cities, industries).
Determinism (nature controls humans): Friedrich Ratzel; popularised by Ellen Churchill Semple and Ellsworth Huntington.
Possibilism (humans choose among nature's possibilities): associated with Vidal de la Blache; the term was coined by Lucien Febvre.
Demographic transition: movement from high birth and death rates (growing population) to low rates (stable population).
Carrying capacity: the maximum population an environment can support.
Sustainable Development Goals: 17 goals adopted by the UN in 2015 for 2030 (e.g. climate action, quality education, gender equality, good health and well-being).

topics.name: Environmental Laws, Institutions & Constitution
topics.summary: Indian environmental Acts with years, constitutional provisions, NGT, NBA, ENVIS, ministries.
points: Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972; Water Act 1974; Forest (Conservation) Act 1980; Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1981 — amended in 1987 to include noise; Environment (Protection) Act 1986; Biological Diversity Act 2002; Forest Rights Act 2006 (tribal and forest dwellers); National Green Tribunal Act 2010.
42nd Amendment (1976) added Article 48A (the State shall protect and improve the environment) and Article 51A(g) (citizens' duty to protect nature).
National Biodiversity Authority (NBA), Chennai, was set up under the Biological Diversity Act.
National Green Tribunal: principal bench in New Delhi; zonal benches in Bhopal, Pune, Kolkata and Chennai; decides environmental cases quickly.
ENVIS: Environmental Information System, a network of centres under the Ministry of Environment.
The Ministry of Environment and Forests was created in 1985; renamed MoEFCC in 2014.
Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) was set up in 1974 under the Water Act.
mistakes: Mixing up Act years — make a one-line list and revise it on exam day.

topics.name: Environmental Movements, Ethics & Justice
topics.summary: Chipko, Appiko, Silent Valley and other movements; views of nature; environmental ethics and justice.
points: Chipko (Uttarakhand, 1973): Chandi Prasad Bhatt, Sunderlal Bahuguna, Gaura Devi.
Appiko (Karnataka, 1983): Panduranga Hegde. Bishnoi sacrifice (1730): Amrita Devi.
Silent Valley (Kerala): the valley of the Kunthipuzha river; the movement stopped a hydro project.
Narmada Bachao Andolan: Medha Patkar, Baba Amte.
Views of nature: Indian/Eastern (nature as mother, to be respected), Western (dominion over nature); ecofeminism arose as an alternative to patriarchal domination of nature.
Anthropocentrism (humans matter most) vs biocentrism (all living beings have value) vs ecocentrism (whole ecosystems have value).
Environmental justice: no group should bear an unfair share of environmental harm; holding meetings in remote places or using only English material excludes people (procedural injustice).
Stewardship: a sense of responsibility for caring for nature.

topics.name: Environment & Human Health
topics.summary: WHO definition of health, aetiology and epidemiology, genetic and behavioural influences on disease.
points: WHO: health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.
Aetiology: the study of the cause (origin) of disease. Epidemiology: the study of how diseases spread in populations.
Genetic diseases: haemophilia, sickle-cell anaemia, thalassaemia, Down's syndrome (mongolism).
Behavioural influences: smoking, tobacco chewing, alcoholism, diet, lack of exercise.
Malaria is infectious (a parasite spread by mosquitoes), not genetic.
